package_info.package_versions: Ubuntu: <=0.105-26ubuntu1.1, Debian: <=0.105-31, CentOS/Fedora/RHEL: all versions prior to vendor patch (see advisories)
package_info.why_malicious: The pkexec binary in PolicyKit is vulnerable to a local privilege escalation (CVE-2021-4034, 'PwnKit') that allows unprivileged users to execute arbitrary code as root by manipulating environment variables, leading to arbitrary library loading and root access. This vulnerability enables attackers to bypass normal privilege boundaries and gain full control over the system.

required_permissions: filesystem (write access to drop malicious .so file)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the attacker sets the SHELL environment variable to the path of an attacker-controlled .so file, then executes /usr/bin/pkexec. pkexec interprets the SHELL variable and loads the specified shared object as root, resulting in execution of attacker code with elevated privileges.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Setting the SHELL environment variable to a path referencing a shared object file is not a legitimate use case and is a direct exploitation of the pkexec vulnerability to achieve privilege escalation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, pkexec should only use the SHELL variable to select a valid shell binary, not to load arbitrary shared objects or execute attacker-controlled code as root.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of pkexec involves running authorized commands as root, with SHELL set to a valid shell path (e.g., /bin/bash), never to a .so file.
key_indicators: SHELL environment variable set to a file with .so extension
pkexec executed by a non-root user
pkexec process loading a shared object from a user-writable location
Resulting process gains root privileges unexpectedly

required_permissions: filesystem (write access to drop malicious .so file)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the attacker sets the CHARSET environment variable to the path of an attacker-controlled .so file, then executes /usr/bin/pkexec. pkexec processes the CHARSET variable and loads the specified shared object as root, resulting in execution of attacker code with elevated privileges.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Manipulating the CHARSET environment variable to reference a shared object file is abnormal and exploits the pkexec vulnerability to load and execute arbitrary code as root.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: pkexec should only use CHARSET to specify character encoding, not to load or execute code from arbitrary file paths.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: CHARSET is legitimately used to set character encoding (e.g., UTF-8), never as a path to a shared object.
key_indicators: CHARSET environment variable set to a file with .so extension
pkexec executed by a non-root user
pkexec process loading a shared object from a user-writable location

required_permissions: filesystem (write access to drop malicious .so file or binary in custom directory)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the attacker sets the PATH environment variable to include a directory containing an attacker-controlled .so file or binary, then executes /usr/bin/pkexec. pkexec uses the manipulated PATH to locate and load the attacker's code as root, resulting in privilege escalation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Altering the PATH environment variable to include a directory with a malicious shared object or binary is a known privilege escalation vector, especially when targeting SUID-root binaries like pkexec.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: PATH should be used to locate legitimate executables, not to facilitate loading of attacker-controlled code as root.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: PATH is legitimately used to control command lookup order, but not for injecting shared objects or binaries for SUID-root execution.
key_indicators: PATH environment variable includes user-writable or non-standard directory
pkexec executed by a non-root user
pkexec process loads or executes code from attacker-controlled location

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious shared object (.so) file containing code designed to execute with root privileges.
Attacker sets environment variables (SHELL, CHARSET, or PATH) to reference the malicious .so file or directory and executes /usr/bin/pkexec.
attack_chain.leads_to: pkexec loads and executes the attacker's code as root

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in the .so file runs with root privileges, enabling privilege escalation and potential full system compromise.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains root access and can perform further malicious actions

behavioral_signatures: Execution of /usr/bin/pkexec by non-root users with environment variables SHELL, CHARSET, or PATH set to values referencing .so files or non-standard directories
pkexec process spawning with environment variables containing file paths ending in .so or pointing to user-writable locations
Unexpected shared object loading by pkexec, especially from non-system directories
pkexec process resulting in new root-level processes not associated with legitimate administrative actions
file_indicators: Presence of attacker-controlled .so files in user-writable directories (e.g., /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm)
pkexec executed from non-standard locations or with manipulated environment variables
Unusual .so files with recent modification times in temporary directories
network_indicators: None inherent to the exploit itself, but post-exploitation activity may include outbound connections from root-owned processes or unexpected network activity initiated by pkexec child processes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor executions of /usr/bin/pkexec by non-root users, focusing on cases where the SHELL, CHARSET, or PATH environment variables are set to suspicious values (such as paths to .so files or user-writable directories). Alert on pkexec processes with these environment variables present, and investigate any shared object files in world-writable or temporary directories. Use EDR or kernel-level monitoring to detect abnormal privilege escalations, SUID binary abuse, and unexpected root process creation. Correlate with file system monitoring for creation or modification of .so files in non-standard locations.
